newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Ericsson, Nokia stock rises briefly on Motorola Q4.
newsitem.headline: Ericsson, Nokia stock rises briefly on Motorola Q4.

text.p: Shares in telecommunications groups AB LM Ericsson of Sweden and Finland's Nokia Oy rose early on Friday after Motorola's earnings report, but later slipped as analysts played down the significance for its Nordic rivals.
For Ericsson and Nokia, the most important parts of the Motorola report late on Thursday covered an upturn in the mobile systems and mobile phone sectors, analysts said.
The U.S. company said that sales at its General Systems Segment, which includes wireless phone infrastructure and handsets, rose 17 percent in the fourth quarter from last year.
Early on Friday, Ericsson shares were up two crowns and Nokia up 8.5 markkaa but analysts were unimpressed and investors' enthusiasm soon waned.

"There were no negative signals about the mobile handset and mobile systems markets and the report merely confirmed what everyone really knew," said Ulf Hellzen, analyst at Stockholm banking group Swedbank.
Reflecting that view, shares quickly came off morning highs.
At 1300 GMT, Ericsson was at 230 crowns ($33.40), down two, while Nokia was up 4.5 markka at 297 markka ($63.20).
"Motorola's success on mobile networks in Asia means Ericsson and Nokia will see a margin squeeze already in 1997," said Lauri Rosendahl, analyst with Aros brokerage in Helsinki.

But most analysts shrugged off Motorola's possible recovery in the mobile handset market. This had been expected as the company had performed so poorly in this area in the first three quarters of the year.
"Market share will swing back and forward depending on where in the product lanching cycle companies are," said Gunnar Andersson, analyst at banking group Handelsbanken in Stockholm.
"The company that launches a new phone can take market share," he said.

Motorola did not give any figures for mobile phone market share. But it introduced a GSM version of its tiny StarTAC phone in Europe in the fourth quarter and although this is a high-end rather than a bulk product, it raised Motorola's overall image, according to Rosendahl.
Market share is not that crucial, however, analysts said.
"The total market, to forecast what happens next, is most important," said London-based Neil Barton of Merrill Lynch .
"Ericsson has read the market very well in the past two years. Nokia has read it extremely well in 1996 and I think it will do even better in 1997."
Analysts said it was difficult to compare Motorola's business with that of its Nordic rivals.
"(For example) Motorola showed that Japanese sales fell, but we would be very surprised if Ericsson showed anything but Japanese sales being up sharply," Barton said.

Motorola's total sales in the fourth quarter rose five percent to $7.69 billion from $7.30 billion in the same period a year ago, while earnings per share dropped to 39 cents from 72 cents, which was lower than expectations of 41 cents. ($1=6.882 Swedish Crown) ($1=4.70 Markka)
